newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria directs oil windfall at economy.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria directs oil windfall at economy.

text.p: Finance Minister Anthony Ani said on Thursday at least part of Nigeria's windfall from high crude oil prices would be directed into the economy instead of paying off mounting external debts.
Ani said after the half-yearly review of progress on the budget up to June 30 that the African oil giant had earned $3.493 billion from crude sales, compared to a budgeted amount of $2.640 billion.
"It is true that we are selling oil at an increased price. Some of this money, amounting to $569 million, is being kept in the nation's reserve account," Ani told journalists.
"Part of it, $264 million, will be used to reactivate the country's railways, and not to service debts," he added.
Ani did not say what would happen to the rest of the excess earned in the period, when crude oil prices averaged $19.43 per barrel against a budget estimate of $16.00 per barrel.

In the first half of 1996 Nigeria kept strictly to its budget plan, spending 22 billion naira ($1.0 billion at the official exchange rate) out of the total $2.0 billion earmarked for foreign debt repayments.
At the end of 1995 Nigeria's total foreign debt had stood at $32.585 billion -- higher than a year before in spite of a $2.0 billion payment and no new loans.
Sixty-five percent is owed to the Paris Club and therefore open to rescheduling.
But Nigeria has not yet met economic conditions leading to talks about rescheduling, although it is working on a Medium Term Economic Strategy (MTES) to satisfy Bretton-Woods institutions.
"Our MTES has now been completed but certain areas need to be further discussed with government before it is finalised," said Ani.
Sticky areas are dual exchange rates, interest rate caps and subsidies on fertiliser and fuel.
The economic crisis in Nigeria has shadowed the political crisis which began in 1993 with the annulment of elections by a former military government that would have ended a decade of army rule.
Military ruler General Sani Abacha's tight fiscal policies aimed at reducing inflation are having success, bringing the year-on-year figure to 31 percent in May from 70 percent a year earlier.
But manufacturers are calling for reflationary measures to boost sagging demand, and Ani on Thursday promised Nigeria would meet its target of 4.94 percent growth for 1996.

In the drive for revenue, Nigeria is pumping oil as fast as it can while strong oil prices continue. A source at one Nigerian producer said his company had been told by the government to produce "flat out" in August and September.
A Reuter survey showed Nigeria pumped an average 2.05 million barrels per day in August, compared to an OPEC quota of 1.865 million barrels a day.
As much as 95 percent of Nigeria's export earnings come from crude oil.
